title: The Malolos Republic
subtitle: Asia's first constitutional republic, and the deal made behind its back.
objectives: Describe the Malolos Congress and who sat in it
State what the Malolos Constitution established
Explain the mock Battle of Manila and why it happened
Explain what the Treaty of Paris did to the new republic
Assess what the First Republic achieved before the war

cards.title: Declaring independence is the easy part
cards.text: Anyone can announce a country. Writing a constitution, opening a congress and running a government is the hard work, and it took five months.

cards.title: June 1898 to January 1899
cards.text: Tap through. Two quiz questions come from these dates.

cards.title: The Malolos Congress
cards.text: It opened on 15 September at Barasoain Church in Bulacan. Most of the men in it were lawyers, doctors and writers.
points: **It ratified the June declaration** of independence.

question.text: Where did the Malolos Congress meet?
question.explain: Barasoain Church in Malolos, Bulacan. Kawit is where independence was declared in June.

cards.title: The Malolos Constitution
cards.text: Approved on 20 January and in force from the 21st. It set out a democratic republic with three branches of government.
points: **Separation of church and state** — passed by one vote.
**The assembly held the most power**, not the president.

cards.title: A constitution is a rule set, written down first
cards.text: Before anyone plays, somebody decides what counts as legal, who can change the rules, and how disputes get settled.

question.text: Which principle passed the Malolos Congress by a single vote?
question.explain: One vote. After three centuries of friar power it was the most contested article in the document.

cards.title: Good spot to pause
cards.text: The republic is built. Part 2 is the two events that undid it. Your place is saved.

cards.title: Two things happened that nobody told the Filipinos about
cards.text: One was a battle that was arranged in advance. The other was a treaty signed on the other side of the world.

cards.title: The mock Battle of Manila
cards.text: Spain and the United States secretly agreed to stage a battle. Spain could then surrender to Americans, not Filipinos.
points: **Filipino forces were kept out of the city.**
**They had been besieging it for months.**

cards.title: It was a fixed fight, in the exact sense
cards.text: Both corners agreed the result before the bell. The people who had done the actual work were not allowed in the building.
points: **Filipinos had done the fighting** for months.

question.text: Why was the Battle of Manila staged?
options: So Spain could surrender to the Americans, not to Filipinos
Because Spain had already left the city
To end the war more quickly
question.explain: Spanish pride, American convenience, and Filipino exclusion. All three at once.

cards.title: The Treaty of Paris
cards.text: Spain handed the islands to the United States for twenty million dollars. The republic in Malolos was not consulted or mentioned.
points: **A congress was sitting in Malolos** at the time.
**None of that appeared in the treaty.**

cards.title: Two accounts of the same year
cards.text: In Manila, 1898 is a war won. In Malolos, it is a republic founded. Both are true and neither side is describing the other.
points: **Whose account gets written down** decides history.
**The treaty is the American version**, in law.
**Both documents exist.** Only one was enforced.

cards.title: What it actually achieved
cards.text: It lasted weeks before the war began, and it is still one of the most significant things in Philippine history.
points: **It wrote a real constitution**, not a proclamation.
**It proved the claim** that Spain had denied for centuries.

question.text: The Malolos Republic was recognised in the Treaty of Paris.
question.explain: False. It was not mentioned at all. Spain and the United States negotiated alone.

terms.def: The assembly that opened 15 September 1898 at Barasoain Church.
Approved 20 January 1899. Established a democratic republic with three branches.
The main drafter of the Malolos Constitution.
Passed at Malolos by a single vote.
13 August 1898. A staged battle so Spain could surrender to Americans.
10 December 1898. Spain sold the islands to the United States for $20 million.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **The Battle of Manila was arranged in advance.**
**The Treaty of Paris never mentioned the republic.**

quiz.text: When and where did the Malolos Congress open?
quiz.explain: 15 September 1898. Kawit in June was the declaration of independence.
quiz.objective: Describe the Malolos Congress and who sat in it

quiz.text: Who mostly made up the Malolos Congress?
quiz.explain: The educated class from Week 2. That shaped what the constitution looked like.
quiz.objective: Describe the Malolos Congress and who sat in it

quiz.text: Who drafted most of the Malolos Constitution?
quiz.explain: Calderon wrote the main draft. Paterno presided over the Congress itself.
quiz.objective: State what the Malolos Constitution established

quiz.text: What did the Malolos Constitution establish?
options: A democratic republic with three branches of government
A monarchy under a Filipino king
A province of the United States
quiz.explain: Executive, legislative and judicial, with the assembly holding the most power.
quiz.objective: State what the Malolos Constitution established

quiz.text: Which article passed by a single vote?
quiz.explain: After three centuries of friar power, it was the most fiercely argued article in the document.
quiz.objective: State what the Malolos Constitution established

quiz.text: When was the First Philippine Republic inaugurated?
quiz.explain: 23 January 1899, at Barasoain Church. The first constitutional republic in Asia.
quiz.objective: Assess what the First Republic achieved before the war

quiz.text: Why was the Battle of Manila in August 1898 staged?
options: So Spain could surrender to Americans instead of Filipinos
Because there were no Spanish troops left
quiz.explain: It preserved Spanish honour and kept Filipino forces out of the city they had been besieging.
quiz.objective: Explain the mock Battle of Manila and why it happened

quiz.text: Filipino forces were allowed into Manila after the staged battle.
quiz.explain: False. They were kept out, despite having besieged the city for months.
quiz.objective: Explain the mock Battle of Manila and why it happened

quiz.text: What did the Treaty of Paris do?
options: Spain transferred the Philippines to the United States for $20 million
quiz.explain: Signed 10 December 1898, with no Filipino present and no mention of the republic.
quiz.objective: Explain what the Treaty of Paris did to the new republic

quiz.text: The Malolos Republic was mentioned in the Treaty of Paris.
quiz.explain: False. A functioning congress was sitting in Malolos and the treaty ignored it entirely.
quiz.objective: Explain what the Treaty of Paris did to the new republic

quiz.text: Why is the Malolos Republic historically significant?
options: It was the first constitutional republic in Asia
It was recognised by every major power
quiz.explain: It lasted weeks before the war, and it is still the first of its kind in Asia.
quiz.objective: Assess what the First Republic achieved before the war

items: The Treaty of Paris is signed
quiz.explain: June, August, September, December 1898. Four events in seven months.
quiz.objective: Explain what the Treaty of Paris did to the new republic

teacher.summary: Week 6 Social Studies continues the revolution topic into the Malolos Republic, matching the Term 1 weekly scope. Week 5 got as far as the inauguration; this lesson is what the republic actually built and what was done to it. Two events are given the weight they deserve and are usually skipped: the mock Battle of Manila, which was a genuine prior arrangement rather than a historian's interpretation, and the Treaty of Paris, which never mentions the republic that was sitting in session at the time. The boxing card is precise rather than decorative — a fixed fight is exactly what August 1898 was. The closing card is deliberately a verdict, because the obvious reading, that a republic lasting weeks achieved nothing, is wrong.
discussion: Ask what the difference is between declaring a country and running one. The five-month timeline answers it.
Ask why separation of church and state was the hardest article to pass. Three centuries of friar power is the answer.
Ask how it feels to besiege a city for months and be kept out of the surrender.
Ask whether a republic that lasted weeks counts. There is a real argument, and both sides are defensible.
teacher.extension: Have him compare the three branches in the Malolos Constitution with the three branches in the Philippines today, and note one difference. The assembly's dominance over the president is the interesting one.
misconceptions: 'Independence in June 1898 meant the Philippines was independent.' No other country recognised it, and Spain sold the islands six months later.
'The Battle of Manila was a real battle.' It was arranged in advance between Spain and the United States.
'The Malolos Republic had no constitution.' It had a full written constitution, approved January 1899.
'The republic achieved nothing because it was short.' It was the first constitutional republic in Asia and it founded a university.
